questions.text:
'The classroom buzzed with nervous energy as students shuffled papers and exchanged worried glances.'

The mood created in this sentence is best described as:
questions.markingGuide: The correct answer is 'Anxious and tense'. Words like 'nervous energy', 'shuffled', and 'worried glances' all contribute to an anxious, tense atmosphere.

questions.text:
'Her words cut through the silence like a knife.'

This is an example of:
questions.markingGuide: The correct answer is Simile. The comparison uses 'like' to compare the effect of her words to a knife cutting through silence.

questions.text:
Read this passage:

'Grandad's workshop smelled of sawdust and stories. Every shelf held a memory — the wooden boat he carved for Mum, the chess set with the missing knight, the half-finished picture frame that would never be completed now.'

What do we learn about Grandad from this description? Use evidence from the text.
questions.markingGuide: 1 mark: Grandad was skilled with his hands/a craftsman (carved boats, chess sets, picture frames). 1 mark: He is likely deceased ('would never be completed now'); he was a family man who made things for loved ones; the workshop preserves his memory/legacy. Accept any reasonable inference supported by text evidence.

questions.text: In the passage above, 'smelled of sawdust and stories' uses:
questions.markingGuide: The correct answer is 'Alliteration and metaphor'. Alliteration: 'sawdust and stories' (repeated 's' sound). Metaphor: a workshop cannot literally smell of 'stories' — this is a figurative way of saying the place is full of memories.

questions.text:
Read this advertisement text:

'Tired of soggy sandwiches? Sick of the same old lunch? Revolution Wraps are here to rescue your taste buds! Made with 100% natural ingredients and wrapped in our signature whole-grain tortilla, you'll never look at lunch the same way again.'

Identify TWO persuasive techniques used and explain how each one works to persuade the reader.
questions.markingGuide: 1 mark each for technique + explanation. Rhetorical questions ('Tired of...? Sick of...?') — connects with reader's frustration, makes them feel understood; Personification ('rescue your taste buds') — makes the product seem heroic/exciting; Alliteration ('same old') — creates rhythm, memorable; Hyperbole ('never look at lunch the same way again') — exaggerates to create excitement; Appeal to health ('100% natural ingredients') — targets health-conscious buyers.

questions.text: Which of the following is the BEST definition of 'tone' in writing?
options: The topic the writer is discussing
The writer's attitude toward the subject
The feeling the reader gets from the text
The speed at which events happen
questions.expectedAnswer: The writer's attitude toward the subject
questions.markingGuide: The correct answer is 'The writer's attitude toward the subject'. Tone refers to the writer's attitude (e.g. sarcastic, formal, playful), not the mood (reader's feeling) or the topic.

questions.text: Explain the difference between 'mood' and 'tone' in a text. Give a brief example of each.
questions.markingGuide: 1 mark: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject (e.g. sarcastic, serious, playful). 1 mark: Mood is the feeling/atmosphere the text creates for the reader (e.g. tense, peaceful, eerie). Example: A writer might use a humorous tone (their attitude) to create a lighthearted mood (reader's feeling). Accept any clear distinction with valid examples.

questions.text:
Read this extract:

'The Waiting Room

Plastic chairs in rows like soldiers,
the clock's tick marking time
like a heartbeat slowing down.
A child builds towers from magazines
while her mother stares at the door —
that door which swallows people whole
and sometimes spits them back
changed.

We sit in the fluorescent glow,
strangers sharing the same silence,
the same prayers we won't say aloud.'

How does the poet create a sense of tension and shared human experience in this poem? In your answer, discuss:
• the use of simile and metaphor
• the contrast between the child and the adults
• how the ending brings the people together.
questions.markingGuide: 4 marks total. 1 mark: similes/metaphors ('chairs like soldiers' — rigid, orderly, waiting for orders; 'clock's tick like a heartbeat slowing down' — time feels heavy, suggests life/death anxiety; 'door which swallows people whole' — hospital/doctor as something frightening, consuming). 1 mark: contrast (child innocently building towers — unaware of seriousness; mother staring at door — consumed by worry; innocence vs anxiety). 1 mark: ending ('strangers sharing the same silence, the same prayers') — despite being strangers, they share the same fear and hope; universal human experience of waiting/worry. 1 mark: quality — how these features work together to build tension while showing common humanity in a medical waiting room.
